title_en: Zhang Shaoheng v. Cangzhou Tianba Agricultural Machinery Co., Ltd. and Zhu Zhanfeng — dispute over infringement of trademark rights
ruling_gist_en: In the context of co-ownership of trademark rights, the licensing of trademark rights should follow the principle of party autonomy, and be exercised by co-owners through consensus; if consensus cannot be reached and there is no justifiable reason, any co-owner shall not prevent other co-owners from licensing the trademark to others through ordinary licensing.

full_text_en:
Zhang Shaohang v. Cangzhou Tianba Agricultural Machinery Co., Ltd. and Zhu Zhanfeng — dispute over trademark infringement

[Ruling Summary]

In the case of co-ownership of a trademark right, the licensing of the trademark right shall follow the principle of party autonomy and be exercised upon consensus among the co-owners. If consensus cannot be reached and there is no justifiable reason, no single co-owner may prevent other co-owners from licensing the trademark to others by way of a non-exclusive license.

Civil Ruling of the Supreme People's Court

(2015) Min Shen Zi No. 3640

Applicant for Retrial (Plaintiff at first instance, Appellant at second instance): Zhang Shaohang, male, Han ethnicity, born on May 16, 1947, residing in Hejian City, Hebei Province.

Agent ad litem: Li Chengdao, lawyer of Hebei Hengtai Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Chen Wei, lawyer of Hebei Hengtai Law Firm.

Respondent (Defendant at first instance, Appellee at second instance): Cangzhou Tianba Agricultural Machinery Co., Ltd. Domicile: Hejian City, Hebei Province.

Legal representative: Zhu Zhancang, Chairman of the company.

Respondent (Defendant at first instance, Appellee at second instance): Zhu Zhanfeng, male, Han ethnicity, born on June 3, 1963, residing in Hejian City, Hebei Province.

The applicant for retrial, Zhang Shaohang, dissatisfied with the civil judgment (2015) Ji Min San Zhong Zi No. 79 rendered by the Hebei High People's Court in the case of dispute over trademark infringement against the respondents Cangzhou Tianba Agricultural Machinery Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Tianba Company) and Zhu Zhanfeng, filed an application for retrial with this Court. This Court formed a collegial panel according to law to review this case. The review has now been concluded.

Zhang Shaohang alleged in his application for retrial: (1) The court of second instance found the basic facts without sufficient evidence. A. Zhang Shaohang and Zhu Zhanfeng jointly established Cangzhou Kefeng Agricultural Machinery Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Kefeng Company) in April 2009. Due to conflicts between the parties, the company could not continue its operations, and the two parties liquidated Kefeng Company. During the liquidation dispute of Kefeng Company, with the mediation of the Hejian City People's Court of Hebei Province, Zhang Shaohang and Zhu Zhanfeng reached a mediation agreement, and the court issued the (2011) He Min Qing Zi No. 1452 civil mediation document. The mediation document clearly stipulated that the "Tianba" trademark was jointly owned by Zhang Shaohang and Zhu Zhanfeng. After the liquidation of Kefeng Company, Zhang Shaohang learned that before the liquidation of Kefeng Company, Zhu Zhanfeng, taking advantage of his position as legal representative of Kefeng Company and without Zhang Shaohang's knowledge, arbitrarily transferred the "Tianba" trademark to Tianba Company, which was established by Zhu Zhanfeng. For this reason, Zhang Shaohang filed a lawsuit with the court against Zhu Zhanfeng's unauthorized transfer of the trademark, requesting confirmation that the transfer was invalid. This case was adjudicated by the Cangzhou Intermediate People's Court, the Hebei High People's Court, and the Supreme People's Court, which held that Zhu Zhanfeng's unauthorized transfer of the "Tianba" trademark was invalid. Since Zhu Zhanfeng, without the consent of the co-owner of the trademark right, arbitrarily transferred the "Tianba" trademark to Tianba Company for use to date, this infringed upon Zhang Shaohang's lawful rights and interests. Based on this, Zhang Shaohang filed this lawsuit, requesting Zhu Zhanfeng and Tianba Company to cease the infringement and compensate for losses. This request should be supported. B. The courts of first and second instance, based on Article 3 of the mediation document, found that Zhang Shaohang could not claim "any rights beyond those agreed in the agreement" against Zhu Zhanfeng, and therefore did not support Zhang Shaohang's claims. This is a subjective assumption. (2) The court of second instance incorrectly applied the law. As a co-owner of the trademark right, Zhu Zhanfeng had no right to unilaterally license the "Tianba" trademark to Tianba Company. If a co-owner of a trademark right could arbitrarily license the use of the registered trademark to others, it could easily lead to abuse of the licensed trademark, ultimately resulting in the loss of the trademark's goodwill value, which is detrimental to protecting the interests of other co-owners of the trademark right. Therefore, restricting a co-owner of a trademark right from arbitrarily licensing the use of the trademark to others serves the common interests of all co-owners in the long run. Thus, neither Zhang Shaohang nor Zhu Zhanfeng has the right to unilaterally license the use of the "Tianba" trademark to others. Even if a co-owner of a trademark right had the right to unilaterally license the use of the registered trademark to others, it must be done with the permission of the trademark owner, by entering into a licensing contract, and by completing the filing procedures. In this case, Zhang Shaohang had reason to believe that Tianba Company's use of the "Tianba" trademark was not licensed by any trademark owner and constituted infringement, for which it should bear tort liability. In summary, Zhang Shaohang requested this Court to revoke the judgments of first and second instance, retry this case, and amend the judgment to support his claims at first instance.

The respondents Zhu Zhanfeng and Tianba Company submitted their opinions: (1) The civil mediation document of the Hejian City People's Court of Hebei Province clearly stated that the RMB 18 million paid by Zhu Zhanfeng to Zhang Shaohang included all business income since the establishment of Kefeng Company, as well as all business income of the newly established Tianba Company up to the date of the agreement. The mediation document divided the property of both Kefeng Company and Tianba Company, effectively treating Tianba Company as a company operated by Zhu Zhanfeng and Zhang Shaohang. (2) Article 3 of the mediation document stipulated that "Zhang Shaohang expresses understanding for any business conduct of Zhu Zhanfeng and waives any rights beyond those agreed in this agreement. Zhang Shaohang undertakes not to pursue any liability of Zhu Zhanfeng in any manner or to raise any claims against him in any manner." Since Zhang Shaohang had already undertaken in the mediation document not to pursue any liability of Zhu Zhanfeng in any manner, Zhang Shaohang's subsequent claim that Zhu Zhanfeng and Tianba Company infringed the trademark and sought damages cannot stand. (3) Tianba Company's use of the "Tianba" trademark does not constitute infringement. Zhu Zhanfeng, as a co-owner of the "Tianba" trademark, has the right to use the trademark, and Tianba Company, owned by Zhu Zhanfeng, naturally also has the right to use the "Tianba" trademark. In fact, Hebei Shengniu Agricultural Machinery Co., Ltd., which was established by Zhang Shaohang, also uses the "Tianba" trademark. In summary, they requested this Court to reject Zhang Shaohang's application for retrial.

This Court holds that during the hearing at second instance, Zhang Shaohang clarified that his claim in the lawsuit was that, after Zhang Shaohang and Zhu Zhanfeng reached the mediation agreement, Tianba Company's use of the "Tianba" trademark without permission constituted infringement. Therefore, the issues in dispute in this case are: (A) Whether the aforementioned use of the trademark by Tianba Company was licensed by Zhu Zhanfeng; (B) Whether the aforementioned use of the trademark by Tianba Company infringed Zhang Shaohang's exclusive right to use the registered trademark.

(A) Regarding Zhang Shaohang's claim that Tianba Company's use of the "Tianba" trademark was not licensed and not filed.

This Court holds that the effective judgment of the court has confirmed that Zhu Zhanfeng's unauthorized transfer of the "Tianba" trademark to the name of Tianba Company was invalid, and the "Tianba" trademark is jointly owned by Zhang Shaohang and Zhu Zhanfeng. Tianba Company was established by Zhu Zhanfeng, and Zhu Zhanfeng once served as the legal representative of Tianba Company. As a co-owner of the "Tianba" trademark, Zhu Zhanfeng also stated during the litigation that he licensed Tianba Company to use the "Tianba" trademark. Whether a licensing contract and filing exist between Zhu Zhanfeng and Tianba Company does not change this fact. Moreover, whether a trademark licensing contract is filed does not affect the validity of the licensing act, but only renders it ineffective against a bona fide third party. Therefore, it can be determined that Tianba Company's use of the "Tianba" trademark was licensed by the co-owner of the trademark right, Zhu Zhanfeng. Zhang Shaohang's ground for retrial on this point cannot stand and is not supported by this Court.

(B) Whether the aforementioned use of the trademark by Tianba Company infringed Zhang Shaohang's exclusive right to use the registered trademark.

As stated above, Tianba Company's use of the "Tianba" trademark was licensed by the co-owner of the trademark right, Zhu Zhanfeng. Therefore, the key issue in this case is whether Zhu Zhanfeng, as one of the co-owners of the "Tianba" trademark, has the right to unilaterally license the trademark to Tianba Company by way of a non-exclusive license.

With respect to the co-ownership of a trademark right, Article 5 of the Trademark Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Trademark Law) as amended in 2001 provides that two or more natural persons, legal persons, or other organizations may jointly apply to the Trademark Office for the registration of the same trademark and jointly enjoy and exercise the exclusive right to use the trademark. Beyond this, the Trademark Law has no specific provisions on the general rules for the exercise of rights by co-owners of a trademark right. This Court holds that, as a private right, in the case of co-ownership of a trademark right, the rules for the exercise of rights shall follow the principle of party autonomy and be exercised upon consensus among the co-owners. If consensus cannot be reached and there is no justifiable reason, no single co-owner may prevent other co-owners from licensing the trademark to others by way of a non-exclusive license. The reasons are as follows:

First, a trademark can only serve to distinguish the source of goods or services and reflect its true value when it is used in production and business activities, in combination with goods or services. If a registered trademark cannot be used because the co-owners of the trademark right find it difficult to reach a consensus, it may not only fail to reflect the value of the registered trademark, contradicting the legislative intent of the Trademark Law, but also make it difficult to protect the common interests of the co-owners. Second, where a co-owner of a trademark right individually licenses the trademark to others by way of a non-exclusive license, it generally does not affect the interests of other co-owners. Other co-owners may use the trademark themselves or license it to others by way of a non-exclusive license. Such a licensing method should, in principle, be permitted. If a co-owner of a trademark right individually licenses the trademark to others by way of a sole license or an exclusive license, it has a greater impact on the interests of other co-owners and should, in principle, be prohibited. Third, according to the Trademark Law, the licensor shall supervise the quality of the goods on which the licensee uses the licensed trademark, and the licensee shall guarantee the quality of the goods on which the registered trademark is used. Therefore, from the perspective of ensuring the quality of goods and the goodwill of the trademark, a co-owner's individual grant of a non-exclusive license generally does not have a material adverse effect on the interests of other co-owners. Even if a co-owner's individual grant of a non-exclusive license results in a reduction of the trademark's goodwill and damages the interests of other co-owners, this is a risk inherent in the system of co-ownership of trademark rights. Where the co-owners have not agreed on the rules for the exercise of rights, the co-owners should anticipate such risks. Finally, requiring the consent of all co-owners of a trademark right before a non-exclusive license can be granted would undoubtedly increase the cost of trademark licensing and may even prevent the use of some valuable trademarks because the co-owners cannot reach an agreement. In conclusion, where the co-owners of a trademark right have not agreed on the rules for the exercise of rights, a co-owner may generally individually license the use of the trademark to others by way of a non-exclusive license.

Applying the above rules, in this case, Zhu Zhanfeng, as a co-owner of the "Tianba" trademark, had the right to individually license the use of the trademark to Tianba Company by way of a non-exclusive license, and Tianba Company's use of the trademark did not constitute infringement. Furthermore, considering the specific facts of this case, the same conclusion can be reached. The reasons are as follows: First, Tianba Company had close ties with both co-owners Zhang Shaohang and Zhu Zhanfeng. In the mediation agreement reached by the parties, it was expressly provided that the business income of Tianba Company (established by Zhu Zhanfeng) up to the date of the mediation agreement was included in the mediation scope and distributed to Zhang Shaohang, and it was agreed that Tianba Company would belong to Zhu Zhanfeng, that Zhang Shaohang would no longer hold any shares, and that all future business income of Tianba Company would belong to Zhu Zhanfeng. That is to say, after the dissolution of Kefeng Company (jointly established by both parties), the "Tianba" trademark of Kefeng Company was owned jointly by both parties. The mediation agreement also included Tianba Company in the mediation scope, stipulating that Tianba Company belonged to Zhu Zhanfeng. It can be considered that when Zhang Shaohang signed the mediation agreement, he should have anticipated that, given the dissolution of Kefeng Company, Tianba Company might continue to use the "Tianba" trademark in its future business activities, yet the mediation agreement did not contain any prohibition to that effect. Second, the existing evidence in this case only shows that Zhu Zhanfeng licensed the "Tianba" trademark to Tianba Company; there is no evidence that Zhu Zhanfeng licensed the trademark to any other party. This case does not involve any indiscriminate issuance of licenses by Zhu Zhanfeng, nor is there evidence that Tianba Company's use caused a reduction in the trademark's goodwill, thereby damaging Zhang Shaohang's interests. Third, according to the facts found by the court of second instance, Hebei Shengniu Agricultural Machinery Co., Ltd., of which Zhang Shaohang is the legal representative, also uses the "Tianba" trademark. Zhang Shaohang submitted a promotional leaflet of that company in his application for retrial to prove that the company uses the "Deshengniu" trademark. This Court holds that, even assuming the authenticity of this evidence can be confirmed, since the promotional leaflet bears no date, it cannot exclude the possibility that Hebei Shengniu Agricultural Machinery Co., Ltd. once used or simultaneously used the "Tianba" trademark. Therefore, the evidence submitted by Zhang Shaohang cannot overturn the above determination of the court of second instance. In conclusion, the court of second instance correctly held that Tianba Company's use of the "Tianba" trademark after the mediation agreement did not constitute infringement. Zhang Shaohang's related grounds for retrial cannot stand.

With respect to Zhang Shaohang's claim that the courts of first and second instance, based on Article 3 of the mediation document, found that Zhang Shaohang could not claim "any rights beyond those agreed in the agreement" against Zhu Zhanfeng, this reasoning was the primary basis for the court of first instance's finding that Zhu Zhanfeng and Tianba Company did not infringe. The court of second instance has already corrected this reasoning. This Court will not further comment on Zhang Shaohang's claim.

In conclusion, Zhang Shaohang's application for retrial does not meet the circumstances set forth in Article 200 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China. Pursuant to Article 204, Paragraph 1 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the ruling is as follows:

Zhang Shaohang's application for retrial is rejected.

Presiding Judge: Zhou Xiang

Judge: Lang Guimei

Acting Judge: Luo Xia

March 31, 2016
